forces.title: Electrification drives fundamental transformation in power systems
forces.description: Global electricity demand is rapidly increasing due to the electrification of transport (EVs), heating (heat pumps), and industry, as well as significant data center expansion. This shift is fundamentally rewiring the energy system, demanding more grid capacity, storage, and flexibility, and accelerating the transition towards hybrid AC/DC architectures. The power sector must adapt to handle greater volumes of electricity flowing over longer distances and in more directions, necessitating sustained investment in generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Renewables require significantly more grid infrastructure per megawatt
forces.description: The growing share of renewables in the generation mix, projected to reach 70% by 2035, fundamentally alters grid requirements. Renewable assets are often located far from load centers, operate at lower utilization rates, and are more dispersed, multiplying grid connection points. This necessitates substantially more transformer capacity, longer transmission distances, and increased grid interconnection to accommodate intermittent and distributed power flows, adding significant investment needs beyond the rising amount of electricity moved.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Transformer supply constraints threaten grid expansion and project timelines
forces.description: The global transformer market is facing a supercycle with demand significantly outstripping supply, leading to a backlog of over 1,000 GVA by 2024. Lead times have stretched to up to five years, and prices have surged by over 50% since 2021. This scarcity is a binding constraint for the power sector, risking stalled interconnection queues, delayed new capacity additions (including renewables), and pushed-back grid build-out timelines. The shortage is poised to persist into the next decade, implying a limit to the acceleration of renewable and grid replacement projects.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Aging grid infrastructure necessitates significant replacement investment
forces.description: Much of the existing grid infrastructure in Europe and North America has exceeded its typical 25- to 40-year design life, with failure rates climbing after 30 years of operation. Replacement accounts for over 30% of transformer demand, with new units typically larger due to increased power needs. This widespread need for replacement, combined with rising power demand and renewable integration, means sustained grid investment is critical and will directly translate into rising demand for components like transformers, projected to reach €627 billion by 2035.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Power conversion technologies are essential for energy transition success
forces.description: Efficient and reliable power conversion technologies like inverters, rectifiers, and HVDC valves are critical for integrating renewable energy sources, managing energy storage, and electrifying mobility and industry. These components are fundamental to the global energy transition, enabling the necessary conversions between AC and DC power for grid use, EV charging, and high-density applications like data centers. Without these technologies, meeting the rapidly increasing demand for electricity and achieving decarbonization targets would not be possible.
forces.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

forces.title: HVDC technology critical for efficient, long-distance power transmission
forces.description: High-voltage DC (HVDC) valves and transmission lines are increasingly critical for modern power networks, offering higher efficiency and control over high-power transmission. HVDC reduces network losses, supports voltage regulation, and is essential for interconnecting asynchronous grids, particularly for bringing power from remote renewable sources like offshore wind to load centers. The market for HVDC valves is forecast to grow at a 6% CAGR from 2024 to 2030, driven by the deployment of HVDC systems for offshore wind and urban grid connections, making it a key enabler for grid modernization and renewables integration.
forces.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

forces.title: Battery energy storage systems bolster grid stability and flexibility
forces.description: The global Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) power conversion equipment market is expected to triple by 2030, driven by utility-scale expansion across major regions. BESS technology converts DC from batteries to AC for grid-wide activities like peak shaving, frequency regulation, and renewable energy integration. As intermittent power sources (solar, wind) increase, greater BESS capacity is vital for grid stability, improved capacity utilization, flexible dispatch, and monetizing hybrid assets, thereby significantly supporting renewable energy targets and grid resilience.
forces.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

forces.title: UK offshore wind deployment needs to accelerate for energy targets
forces.description: Despite offshore wind generating almost 20% of the UK’s electricity supply in the last year with 17 GW installed capacity, progress needs to accelerate. Only 500 MW was installed in 2025, a rate insufficient to make a material contribution to overall energy targets. While Allocation Round 7 awarded a significant 8 GW, further cost reductions in subsequent rounds are necessary to impact consumer bills and strengthen the UK’s leadership position in the field, indicating a need for faster, more cost-effective deployment.

forces.title: Electrification drives robust European power demand growth
forces.description: After years of stagnation, European power demand is projected to grow robustly from 3,000 TWh in 2025 to 4,300 TWh by 2040. This acceleration is primarily driven by the widespread electrification of transport (140 million EVs), buildings (55 million residential heat pumps), data centers (450 TWh increase), and industrial processes (200 TWh additional consumption). Electricity's share of final energy consumption is expected to rise to 32% by 2040, creating significant upside for the electric power sector and requiring a substantial acceleration in renewable and nuclear supply.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Grid congestion and negative prices hinder renewable power utilization
forces.description: The rapid build-out of intermittent renewables in Europe is creating significant grid congestion and temporal mismatches, leading to record volumes of voluntarily curtailed power and increasingly frequent hours of negative pricing. In 2025, curtailment reached nearly 4 TWh across Germany, France, and the Netherlands, representing an 18% CAGR since 2020. This trend neutralizes cross-border exports and depresses day-ahead prices, indicating a rising premium on solutions like flexibility, storage, demand response, and priority grid access to make clean power usable where and when needed, and acting as a headwind to further renewable deployment.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Generation ownership shifts towards IPPs and prosumers
forces.description: The ownership structure of power generation has significantly diversified, moving away from incumbent utilities towards independent power producers (IPPs) and decentralized asset owners (prosumers). In Germany, utilities' share of installed capacity fell from 82% in 2000 to 26% by 2026, while IPPs grew to 41% and prosumers to 33%. This fragmentation is driven by a more competitive and policy-dependent generation market, with incumbents increasingly prioritizing regulated grid infrastructure over direct investment in generation. This shift requires utilities to adapt to new market dynamics and potentially partner with diverse generation sources.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: AI adoption spurs data center growth, creating new utility demands
forces.description: Accelerating AI adoption is driving rapid expansion of data centers, with Europe's IT capacity expected to double from 20 GW in 2025 to nearly 40 GW by 2030. This growth creates new demands and flexibility value pools for utilities, including orchestrated flexibility, on-site storage solutions extending UPS models, bridge and backup power for early connections, and microgrid services. Utilities must adapt their supply chain strategies, as demand for critical equipment like gas turbines and transformers has sharply increased, with turbine order books extending beyond 2029.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Surging capital costs and unfavorable auctions impede renewable deployment
forces.description: European efforts to diversify energy supply and achieve ambitious renewable targets are clashing with market realities. Surging capital costs, supply chain bottlenecks, and unfavorable auction designs are cooling developer appetite, leading to project economics deteriorating. This friction is evident in failed offshore auction rounds, such as Germany's August 2025 auction for 2.5 GW of capacity and the Netherlands' late-2025 auction for the 1-GW Nederwiek I-A site, which closed without a single bid. Even well-capitalized oil majors are scaling back offshore wind plans, threatening decarbonization goals.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: UK electricity bills to rise, fixed network costs main driver
forces.description: UK consumer electricity bills are projected to rise in nominal terms by £115 (13%) to £996 by 2035 in a central scenario, with fixed network costs driving 86% of this increase. This sustained rise stems from declining demand since 2015 and increasing fixed costs from generation and grid build-out. The UK has the highest electricity-to-gas price ratio in its peer group, largely due to taxes, levies, and gas price pass-through, creating a negative demand/price spiral that will worsen without intervention.
forces.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

forces.title: Industrial demand, especially data centers, key to lowering electricity bills
forces.description: Increasing electricity demand, particularly from industrial sources like data centers, is crucial for cutting UK electricity bills. With forecasts already incorporating ambitious EV and heat pump adoption, data centers represent the most economically additive driver of demand. Delivering 14GW of the current data center pipeline could reduce every household's bill by £35 by 2035, provided projects connect intelligently and operate flexibly, allowing fixed grid investment costs to be spread across a larger usage base, fostering economic growth and supporting AI ambitions.
forces.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

viewpoints.title: Transformer Shortage Reshapes Power Sector Decisions, Stalling Grid and Renewables Growth
viewpoints.description: The global transformer market has entered a supercycle, with demand outrunning supply due to electrification, renewable energy shifts, and aging infrastructure. Transformer lead times have stretched to up to five years, and prices have surged over 50% since 2021. This scarcity is no longer a procurement detail but a strategic imperative for energy infrastructure stakeholders. Utilities and grid operators must secure capacity years ahead, as supply constraints will limit grid build-out and renewable acceleration until the 2030s, potentially increasing energy prices and reducing power access.
viewpoints.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

viewpoints.title: UK Energy Sector Faces Structural Transition Amid Volatility, Diverging Risks
viewpoints.description: The UK energy sector is navigating a complex structural transition, balancing security, affordability, and decarbonization efforts. While oil and gas prices remain elevated due to geopolitical uncertainty, volatility has eased since the 2022-2023 crisis. However, a widening divide exists: larger oil and gas and renewable producers benefit from stronger balance sheets and higher commodity prices, enabling continued investment. Conversely, smaller players, especially retail suppliers, face heightened risk with limited capacity to absorb further cost shocks. Scale and financial resilience are crucial for managing ongoing volatility and investment demands.

viewpoints.title: Power Conversion Market Growth Driven by Electrification, but Solar PV Faces Price Pressure
viewpoints.description: The global power conversion market, essential for electrification and integrating renewables into the grid, is projected to reach $95 billion by 2030. While high-complexity segments like HVDC and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) offer compelling growth, lower-complexity areas such as utility-scale solar PV face price compression and commoditization. This segment is expected to decline by 2% annually through 2030 due to intense competition and market saturation in mature regions like Europe, requiring a focus on cost optimization and differentiated hybrid inverter capabilities.
viewpoints.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

viewpoints.title: UK Electricity Demand Surges, Requiring Major Investment in Generation and Networks
viewpoints.description: The UK is experiencing sustained growth in electricity demand for the first time in over two decades, driven by the electrification of transport, heating, and industry as part of its energy transition. Meeting this increasing demand necessitates significant investment across power generation (especially renewables), networks, storage, and system flexibility to ensure continued affordability, reliability, and availability. This shift underlines electricity's growing importance in the UK's energy mix, despite ongoing reliance on fossil fuels for overall energy consumption.

viewpoints.title: UK Electricity Bills Driven by Fixed Costs; Increased Demand Needed for Reduction
viewpoints.description: Britain's high energy costs are primarily driven by expensive electricity, with domestic prices among the highest in Europe and non-domestic the absolute highest. This is not due to generation costs but rather taxes, levies, and gas price pass-through. Fixed network costs are a major component, and declining demand since 2015 has exacerbated the issue. Counterintuitively, the solution involves increasing electricity usage, particularly through industrial demand like data centers. This would spread fixed grid investment costs over a larger base, potentially cutting household bills by £35 by 2035 and supporting economic growth.
viewpoints.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less
